why: Herr Weber is an adult you don't know well, so you use polite Sie. heißen (with -en) also only fits Sie here; du would need heißt.
en: Mr Weber, what is your name?

why: Lena is a friend, so you say du. The ending -st (kommst) also belongs to du.
en: Hi Lena! Where are you from?

why: You are talking to two friends at once, so "you" is ihr. The ending -t (wohnt) fits ihr.
en: Lena and Jonas, where do you live?

q: Das ist Jonas. ___ wohnt in Köln.
why: Jonas is a man, so the pronoun is er (he). sie would mean "she".
en: This is Jonas. He lives in Cologne.

why: With ich the ending is -e: ich heiße.
en: My name is Jonas. And you?

why: The stem heiß- already ends in ß, so du only adds -t: du heißt (not heißst).
en: What's your name?

why: Malte = er, so the ending is -t. The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so an extra e comes in: er arbeitet.
en: Malte works in Cologne.

why: With du the ending is -st: du wohnst.
en: You live in Hamburg, don't you?

why: The answer aus Hamburg says where someone comes from, so the question word is woher? (where from?).
en: Where does Mr Weber come from? – From Hamburg.

why: German asks for a name with wie (literally "how is he called?"), not was.
en: What's your friend's name? – Jonas.

why: In a W-question the verb comes straight after the question word, then the subject: Wo wohnt Malte?
en: Where does Malte live?

why: The answer is a person, so ask with wer? (who?). Remember: wer is "who", wo is "where".
en: Who lives here? – Mrs Yilmaz.

q: Ich ___ Priya. Ich komme aus Indien.
why: With ich, sein becomes bin: ich bin.
en: I'm Priya. I come from India.

why: Lena und Jonas = sie (they), so sein becomes sind.
en: Lena and Jonas are friends.

why: With ihr, sein becomes seid (with d). seit with t is a different word (since).
en: You're from Mexico, aren't you?

why: With du, sein becomes bist. In a yes/no question it comes first: Bist du …?
en: Are you a student?

why: wir takes the infinitive form, ending in -en: wir wohnen.
en: We live in Berlin.

q: Ihr ___ sehr schnell, Lena und Jonas!
why: ihr takes -t: ihr lernt. Only wir, sie and Sie take -en.
en: You learn very fast, Lena and Jonas!

q: Priya und Malte ___ Englisch und Deutsch.
why: Two people = sie (they), so the verb takes the infinitive form: sie sprechen.
en: Priya and Malte speak English and German.

why: Polite Sie always uses the same form as sie (they), ending in -en: Sie kommen.
en: Mr Weber, where are you from?

why: The answer is ja, so this is a yes/no question: the verb comes first, and with du it ends in -st. A W-question (Wo …?) cannot be answered with ja.
en: Do you live in Berlin? – Yes.

q: ___ Frau Yilmaz zu Hause? – Ja, sie ist da.
why: The verb comes first. Frau Yilmaz = sie, so sein becomes ist.
en: Is Mrs Yilmaz at home? – Yes, she's in.

q: Arbeiten ___ hier, Herr Weber? – Ja, hier in der Schule.
why: After the verb comes the subject. Herr Weber is addressed politely, and arbeiten (-en) fits Sie.
en: Do you work here, Mr Weber? – Yes, here at the school.

q: Kommst du aus Mexiko? – ___, ich komme aus Indien.
why: A yes/no question is answered with ja or nein. The speaker is from India, not Mexico, so: Nein. nicht and kein are not answer words.
en: Are you from Mexico? – No, I come from India.

why: Hier fills position 1, so the verb must come next (position 2) and the subject wir follows it.
en: We learn German here.

why: Priya und Malte together fill position 1. The verb comes next and fits two people: arbeiten. Don't add sie again.
en: Priya and Malte work in Cologne.

why: Englisch is in position 1, so the verb goes to position 2 and the subject (Malte) comes after it.
en: Malte understands English very well.

q: In Hamburg ___ Herr und Frau Weber.
why: In Hamburg is position 1, the verb is position 2. The subject comes after it, and it is two people, so: wohnen.
en: Mr and Mrs Weber live in Hamburg.

why: Malte = er, and haben loses its b: er hat.
en: Malte has two daughters.

why: With du, haben loses its b: du hast (not habst).
en: Do you have time today?

why: German says "I have hunger": Ich habe Hunger. Hunger is a noun, so sein does not work here.
en: I'm hungry.

why: With ihr, haben is habt.
en: You have a daughter? How lovely!

why: Opa (grandpa) is masculine: der Opa. It is the subject here, so der stays der.
en: Grandpa is 80 years old.

why: Freundin is feminine (die Freundin), so "a" is eine.
en: Jonas has a girlfriend.

q: ___ Kinder sind sieben und neun Jahre alt.
why: Kinder is plural, and the plural article is always die, even though it is das Kind in the singular.
en: The children are seven and nine years old.

why: Mädchen is neuter (das Mädchen), even though it means "girl", so "a" is ein.
en: That is a girl.

q: Das ist Lena und das ist ___ Bruder.
why: The owner is Lena (she), so "her" is ihr. Bruder is masculine, so there is no -e.
en: This is Lena and this is her brother.

why: You ask Jonas (du), so "your" is dein. Schwester is feminine, so it takes -e: deine.
en: Jonas, what's your sister's name?

why: To Herr Weber you say Sie, so "your" is Ihr with a capital I. Kinder is plural, so it takes -e: Ihre.
en: Mr Weber, where do your children live?

q: Lena und Jonas, ist das ___ Hund?
why: Talking to two friends (ihr), "your" is euer. Hund is masculine, so there is no ending: euer Hund.
en: Lena and Jonas, is that your dog?

why: Saft is masculine (der Saft) and it is the object of nehmen, so ein becomes einen.
en: I'll have a juice.

why: Banane is feminine: die stays die as an object. Only masculine words change.
en: Malte takes the banana.

why: Here der Salat is the subject (it is very good), so it stays der. den is only for the object.
en: The salad is very good.

why: Bier is neuter (das Bier). Neuter words don't change as an object: ein Bier.
en: Jonas orders a beer.

why: With ich the form is möchte.
en: I'd like two bread rolls, please.

why: er/sie/es has the same form as ich: Lena möchte, with no -t.
en: Lena would like a glass of juice.

why: After möchten the second verb goes to the end as an infinitive, with no zu (no "to").
en: We'd like to pay, please.

why: Polite Sie takes the -en form: Möchten Sie …?
en: Would you like a coffee, Mrs Yilmaz?

why: Kaffee has no article here, so you negate it with kein. It is the masculine object, so kein becomes keinen.
en: No thanks, I don't want any coffee.

why: gut is an adjective, not a noun, so the negation is nicht.
en: The food is not good.

why: Brot has no article here and is neuter (das Brot), so: kein Brot.
en: Sorry, we don't have any bread.

why: To negate a verb (kommen), use nicht. kein only goes with nouns, and nein is the answer word "no".
en: Lena isn't coming today.

why: der Stuhl → die Stühle: it adds -e and an umlaut. German does not add -s here as English does.
en: There are four chairs in the kitchen.

why: die Tür is feminine, and most feminine nouns add -(e)n: die Türen.
en: The room has two doors.

why: Words that end in a vowel and come from other languages add -s: das Sofa → die Sofas.
en: The sofas are new.

why: das Bad is a short neuter noun: it adds -er and an umlaut: die Bäder.
en: The flat has two bathrooms.

q: In der Küche gibt es ___ Kühlschrank.
why: es gibt takes the accusative, so the masculine der Kühlschrank becomes einen Kühlschrank.
en: There is a fridge in the kitchen.

why: es gibt never changes, even for many things: Im Haus gibt es zwei Bäder.
en: There are two bathrooms in the house.

why: It is the same es gibt, turned round for a yes/no question: the verb comes first: Gibt es …?
en: Is there a supermarket here?

why: After es gibt comes the accusative, so der Garten becomes keinen Garten.
en: Unfortunately there's no garden here.

why: After sein the adjective has no ending: Die Küche ist klein.
en: The kitchen is small.

why: Die Zimmer is plural, so sein becomes sind. The adjective hell stays as it is.
en: The rooms are very bright.

q: Der Garten ist ___ groß, aber sehr schön.
why: groß is an adjective, so the negation is nicht, not kein.
en: The garden isn't big, but it's very nice.

why: In a question too, an adjective after sein has no ending.
en: Is the sofa new?

why: einkaufen is separable: kaufen goes in position 2 and ein goes to the end.
en: We're doing the shopping at the supermarket today.

q: Lena ___ heute Abend ihre Oma an.
why: anrufen splits: ruft takes position 2, and an is already at the end.
en: Lena is calling her grandma this evening.

why: mitkommen (to come along) is separable: kommst goes first in the question and mit goes to the very end.
en: Are you coming along to the cinema?

why: fernsehen splits: sieht stands in position 2 (sehen changes to sieht with er), and fern goes to the end.
en: Malte watches TV in the evening.

why: Clock times take um: um halb sieben (6:30).
en: I get up at half past six.

why: Days of the week take am: am Dienstag.
en: I have an appointment on Tuesday.

why: German says am Wochenende (at the weekend), like am Montag.
en: At the weekend I visit my parents.

q: Die Praxis ist von 8 ___ 12 Uhr geöffnet.
why: "From … to" with times is von … bis: von 8 bis 12 Uhr.
en: The doctor's practice is open from 8 to 12.

why: Am Samstag fills position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject (ich) follows it.
en: On Saturday I sleep late.

why: Heute is in position 1, so the verb (hat) comes next and the subject (Malte) after it.
en: Malte doesn't have time today.

why: After the time phrase the verb comes second, then the subject. Jonas und Lena are two people, so: spielen.
en: At the weekend Jonas and Lena play football.

why: Um halb acht (7:30) is position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject (Priya) third.
en: Priya has breakfast at half past seven.

why: fahren changes a → ä with er/sie/es: sie fährt.
en: Priya is going to Cologne tomorrow.

why: sprechen changes e → i with er/sie/es: sie spricht.
en: Lena speaks English very well.

why: lesen changes e → ie with du, and the s of the stem joins the ending: du liest.
en: What do you like reading?

why: The vowel only changes with du and er/sie/es. With ihr, fahren is regular: ihr fahrt.
en: You're driving too fast!

q: Priya ___ Bücher. Das ist ihr Hobby.
why: To say you like doing something, the verb stays in position 2 and gern comes after it: Priya liest gern Bücher.
en: Priya likes reading books. It's her hobby.

q: Ich trinke gern Kaffee, aber ich trinke ___ Tee.
why: gern has its own forms: gern → lieber → am liebsten. gerner does not exist.
en: I like drinking coffee, but I prefer tea.

why: am liebsten means "best of all": Was machst du am liebsten? = What do you like doing best?
en: What do you like doing best? – I dance!

why: For a thing you like, use mögen: ich mag. gern always needs a verb with it: Ich trinke gern Wein.
en: I like wine.

why: After können the second verb goes to the end as an infinitive, without zu.
en: I can dance very well.

why: wollen: er/sie/es will, with no -t (the same as ich will).
en: Jonas wants to play football today.

why: können has a (not ö) with ich, du and er: du kannst.
en: Can you swim?

why: Am Samstag is in position 1, so the modal verb comes next and wir after it. wandern stays at the end.
en: On Saturday we want to go hiking.

q: Der Computer ist gut. Ich kaufe ___.
why: der Computer is masculine and here it is the object of kaufen, so er becomes ihn.
en: The computer is good. I'm buying it.

why: You are the object of anrufen, so du becomes dich.
en: Lena, I'll call you tomorrow.

q: Die Hose ist zu teuer. Ich nehme ___ nicht.
why: die Hose is feminine, so "it" is sie, and sie does not change as an object.
en: The trousers are too expensive. I'm not taking them.

q: Besuchst du ___ am Wochenende? Wir sind zu Hause.
why: wir is the object of besuchen here, so it becomes uns.
en: Are you visiting us at the weekend? We're at home.

why: der Pass is masculine and the object of suchen, and it belongs to Priya (her): ihr + -en = ihren.
en: Priya is looking for her passport.

why: das Fahrrad is neuter, and neuter does not change as an object: dein Fahrrad.
en: Jonas, do you need your bike today?

why: Eltern is plural, and the plural does not change as an object: seine Eltern.
en: Malte is visiting his parents.

why: Polite "your" is Ihr. Schlüssel is masculine and the object, so: Ihren Schlüssel.
en: Mrs Yilmaz, do you have your key?

why: die Jacke is feminine, so welch- takes -e, like die: welche.
en: Which jacket will you take? – This one here.

why: der Computer is masculine and the object of nehmen, so dieser becomes diesen (like der → den).
en: I'll take this computer.

why: das Handy is neuter, so welch- takes -es, like das: welches.
en: Which phone costs 200 euros?

why: Schuhe is plural, so dies- takes -e, like die: diese Schuhe.
en: These shoes are very cheap.

why: To someone you call Sie, the imperative is the infinitive + Sie: Warten Sie!
en: Please wait here, Mrs Yilmaz!

why: To one friend (du), take du kommst and drop du and -st: Komm!
en: Jonas, come quickly!

why: To two friends (ihr), use the ihr form without ihr: ihr seid → Seid leise!
en: Lena and Priya, please be quiet!

why: lesen changes e → ie with du (du liest), and the imperative keeps it: Lies!
en: Read the book, Jonas!

q: Ich fahre mit ___ Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
why: mit always takes the dative: das Fahrrad → mit dem Fahrrad.
en: I cycle to work.

why: To a person or place you go zu. der Arzt is masculine, so zu + dem = zum.
en: Malte is going to the doctor today.

why: For towns and countries without an article, "to" is nach: nach Indien.
en: Priya is flying to India in July.

q: Lena fährt mit ___ Freunden nach Hamburg.
why: mit takes the dative. In the plural, die → den, so ihre → ihren, and the noun adds -n: Freunden.
en: Lena is going to Hamburg with her friends.

why: The answer ins Kino is a direction, so the question is wohin? (where to?).
en: Where are you going? – To the cinema.

why: arbeiten is not a movement; the answer says where Malte is. So ask with wo?
en: Where does Malte work? – In Cologne.

why: The answer aus München tells you where the train comes from, so ask with woher?
en: Where is the train coming from? – From Munich.

why: wo asks where someone is, so the answer is a place: im Supermarkt. Zum Supermarkt would answer wohin?
en: Where is Lena? – At the supermarket.

q: Ich habe Fieber. Ich ___ zu Hause bleiben.
why: With ich, müssen is muss: no ending and no umlaut.
en: I have a temperature. I have to stay at home.

why: After müssen the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive, without zu.
en: Lena has to work a lot today.

q: Ihr ___ morgen um 8 Uhr da sein.
why: With ihr the form is müsst: the umlaut comes back in the plural.
en: You have to be there at 8 tomorrow.

why: Am Sonntag fills position 1, so muss comes second and ich third; arbeiten stays at the end. nicht müssen = not have to.
en: On Sunday I don't have to work.

why: With ich, dürfen is darf: no ending and no umlaut. Darf ich …? = May I …?
en: May I sit here?

why: man (people in general) takes the er/sie/es form: man darf. darf nicht = it is not allowed.
en: You mustn't eat on the bus.

q: Herr Weber, ___ wir jetzt nach Hause gehen?
why: With wir, dürfen keeps its infinitive form: wir dürfen.
en: Mr Weber, may we go home now?

why: After dürfen the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive, without zu.
en: You mustn't do any sport today.

why: The infinitive (gehen) closes the bracket at the very end; time and place go in the middle.
en: I have to go to the chemist's tomorrow.

why: nicht goes in the middle, just before the infinitive. The infinitive is always last.
en: We can't come on Saturday.

why: At the end of a modal sentence a separable verb stays in one piece: fernsehen.
en: Jonas wants to watch TV this evening.

q: Am Montag ___ wieder in die Schule gehen.
why: Am Montag is position 1, so the modal verb (darf) is second and the subject third; gehen is already at the end.
en: On Monday Jonas is allowed to go back to school.

why: Perfekt = haben + Partizip II at the end. kaufen → ge + kauf + t = gekauft.
en: I bought a suitcase.

why: übernachten (stay the night) is not a movement, so it takes haben. With wir: haben.
en: We stayed the night in Hamburg.

why: Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge-: studieren → studiert.
en: Priya studied English in India.

why: Am Wochenende is position 1, so haben comes second, the subject third and the participle last.
en: We had a barbecue at the weekend.

q: Lena und Jonas ___ ans Meer gefahren.
why: fahren is a movement from A to B, so the Perfekt uses sein: sie sind gefahren.
en: Lena and Jonas went to the seaside.

q: Malte ___ gestern lange in der Firma geblieben.
why: bleiben always takes sein in the Perfekt, even though nobody moves.
en: Malte stayed late at work yesterday.

why: lesen is not a movement, so it takes haben: Lena hat gelesen.
en: Lena read a lot on holiday.

q: ___ du schon einmal in Indien gewesen?
why: sein itself takes sein in the Perfekt: Bist du … gewesen? With du: bist.
en: Have you ever been to India?

why: trinken is irregular: the vowel changes to u and the ending is -en: getrunken.
en: I drank a coffee.

why: sehen → gesehen: the vowel stays e, and the ending is -en.
en: Have you seen the film?

why: schreiben → geschrieben: ei becomes ie, and the ending is -en.
en: Malte wrote an email.

q: Wir haben im Hotel sehr gut ___.
why: schlafen → geschlafen: the vowel stays a (no ä), and the ending is -en.
en: We slept very well in the hotel.

why: After am the ordinal ends in -en: am zweiten Juni.
en: Lena's party is on the second of June.

q: ___ März ist es oft noch kalt.
why: For a month (and a season) use im: im März.
en: In March it's often still cold.

why: After der the ordinal ends in -e: der siebte. 7 is special: sieben drops its -en, so siebte.
en: Tomorrow is the seventh of April.

q: Wir fliegen am ___ August nach Indien.
why: 1 is special: erste (first). After am it ends in -en: am ersten August.
en: We're flying to India on the first of August.

why: Weather verbs always have es as their subject: Es regnet.
en: What's the weather like? – It's raining.

why: Weather needs es as the subject. heute is in position 1, so the verb comes next and es follows: Heute ist es kalt.
en: It's very cold today.

why: es takes the er/sie/es form: es regnet. Regen is the noun (rain).
en: In autumn it often rains.

why: Weather with an adjective uses es ist. In a yes/no question the verb comes first: Ist es …?
en: Is it warm today?

q: Wir haben am Freitag für die Party ___.
why: ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: ein + ge + kauft = eingekauft.
en: We did the shopping for the party on Friday.

why: rufen is irregular (gerufen), so anrufen → angerufen: an + ge + rufen.
en: Jonas called his grandma.

why: ankommen is a movement (arriving), so the Perfekt uses sein: ist angekommen.
en: The train arrived on time.

why: einladen → eingeladen: ge- goes after the prefix ein-, and laden keeps its -en ending.
en: Did you invite Lena to the party?
